love the spirituals and the spiritual does so much for me personally and I have found that it has helped others and this is I am one of the few people that really have a chance to do the things that they love

and speaking of recording people say that you have to be in the mood to sing that you can't turn your talent off and on at will is this true well that's the way it is with me well then when you record if you're not in the mood to sing what happens to the recording day just a flop record one you don't like anyway I know uh... could you tell us about it well it's not exactly a school it would be a religious center oh a religious center yeah with the school combined uh huh to teach what for instance uh well as I would like to say in singing I have had contact with so many different people and uh some have been very much perplexed and confused and uh I have found that uh they have told me rather that my singing has been of some type of help to them uh when they were low in spirit that they found that the songs did so much for them but uh being uh a woman that believes in God like I do I I feel that uh if a simple song can do that the training of the mind into the higher realm of salvation uh will help them to live better will you will there be uh music taught there then? yes well Mahalia do you have enough money of your own to complete this project? no I'm trying very hard to raise the money from uh my concerts and I have asked some of my friends like uh Miss Diana Schuh yes and the great Mr. Ben Crosby and the great Mr. Frank Sinatra and well I think they're all gonna help me cause they all love me they're gonna do a show for you or something is it you mean? yeah use the proceeds for the school well that'll be a little some help but it's gonna take a lot of money isn't it? well the type of school must remain owned because we're going to have uh people from their seminary and then uh uh from uh different schools of art to teach and to train our young people I see um uh not only just the same but whatever their line of profession is

would you like to try that? without a doubt I know it I don't have to think about that if jazz can do it I know these spirituals can well I hope you get a chance to try it

people everywhere love to hear you sing? well uh there are a few people that uh you would say that is just mentally sick because um and sickness this mental sickness is just like any other disease and that's why prejudice come in uh because I go down south and even many of the white people there come in and I never question about where uh will the white people sit wherever the color because the gospel is too great for that kind of question to come they might do it to Louis Armstrong or some of the other people but not to Mahaya yeah when they come to hear me they come in to hear the gospel and they sit wherever they can get a seat well Mahaya could you sort of give us a sum up your philosophy of life just briefly do you have one thing? well I believe that uh life is beautiful and it can be beautiful wouldn't you have a quotation of I loved it would you tell it to our audience? well I have many quotations I uh I I could uh the one that it was good that I was afflicted yes yes that's your summation well out of affliction comes uh comes joy come understanding and when one has suffered and had pain they can uh understand you when you are having it

well I understand you I think and I love to hear you sing and thanks for letting us talk to you Mahaya thank you right after this message we'll be joining Jack in Europe for the second half of Here's Hollywood is that right? yes that's right and I am happy well I can see that when you are singing

singing. Oh yes. And one can hear it. Well, why are you so happy? Well, the music makes the soul happy. And I think I sing all the time and it keeps my spirit happy. And you sing at home too? Oh yes. I sing when I'm cooking, when I'm working around the house. I sing so much till the neighbors sometimes come around and listen. So I just sing. It keeps me happy. It helps me to bear the burdens of the day. What do you like to sing the best? Well, I have a number of songs that I love to sing. Some songs are certain moods I'm in. Well, I like to sing that particular song. If I'm in a sad mood, well, I sing a song with a cry. And when I feel happy, jolly, well, I sing a song with a lot of beat and a lot of rhythm to it. Such as, um, when the saints go marching in, um, oh, uh, keep your hands on the plow. Uh, didn't it rain? Songs like that. They are jolly songs, you know. And I just get around the house and
sing them till I sing my blues away. You like to sing those songs with beat, don't you? Oh, yeah, yeah. Now, one other thing about your songs. They're all religious songs, aren't they? Yes,

they are. Well, I am very, I'm, I'm very religious, uh, should I say myself? Um, I'm religious so to the extent that I sacrifice myself, uh, and don't use my voice for anything else but singing religious songs. And, uh, I have a type of voice that I hear people talk about that has a blue note in it. What I mean about a blue note has the, um, the American music like we call the blues blues in America, you know. Well, in other words, it's, it has the cry in it. It has sort of heart, you know. And, of course, all the bands would like for me to sing the blues or the poplar songs. So I am, uh, like some people say, I'm very, I'm over emotional. So I sacrifice and sing nothing but religious songs. And truly, okay, I don't think I could really sing the blues like they think I can. I just might sound like it, but I, I don't think I could. I just love to sing these religious songs because they are part of my, my life. I believe what I'm singing. I believe in these songs. It has done so much for me. And that's why I sing it because it's done so much for me. And I like to sing it because it helps other people. You sing in church too, don't you? Oh yeah. I sing in churches. In fact, I started out in the churches. The church. How was when? Oh, well, I, in fact, I've been singing all my life down in New Orleans. I come from New Orleans, you know. It is known as the home of the jazz in America. But, um, people out there got religion too. And, um, uh, I start singing in the church when I was just about four or five years old.
Well, then you have done some church singing indeed. Now tell me, when you grew up, did you only hear the singing in the church? Or did you also hear the blues singing? Did you hear the jazz?

Oh, yes. I couldn't help from hearing it. I knew all about, um, Louis Armstrong and Papa Celestan. I've seen them all my life. And, uh, uh, Kid Kelly and Buck Johnson and all of them. I, uh, I knew all of those people. And, um, I met them. And they used to go to church too. That's why they can play these religious songs. Like, uh, uh, when the saints and, uh, what this other song, uh, we shall walk the streets of glory. And, uh, just a closer walk with these by and by when the morning comes. Because they were brought up in that. There isn't very much different in music. All music is basically the same thing. There isn't but 88 keys on the keyboard. So, you, it is too much different. But the difference in the music is one is reverence to God. And another, well, people might say it's to the devil. But some people just sing, uh, when they're happy, maybe folk songs. You know, they get around the, like down in New Orleans, you know, in the wintertime, we used to be on the levee. The correct word, I think, is used, dike. But we used to get on the levee. That's the high amount of ground that, uh, divides, uh, to protect you from the Mississippi River. You know? We used to, we used to get there. And, uh, we used to sit out there on the levee near the railroad track, the Mississippi River and the levee and the railroad track. And we would just make up songs. They weren't bad songs. We used to, we just made them up to amuse ourselves. We, we weren't rich and we couldn't go to nightclubs, uh, things like that. So we just sat as kids and made up songs and sang by the far. Uh, and, uh, used to eat popcorns and sugar cans and things like that. Had a glorious time. Now tell me, are you still making up songs? Yes. Yeah. I, I, uh, write most of my own songs. That's what I understand. That's what I ask. And can't read a lick of music. No? No. Don't know how to, uh, I don't know how to sight read. I never had a day's lesson in my life. But, uh, I, uh, I hear music. I can hear it. And as I hear it, I sing it that way. And folk thinks it's all right.

Well, I can see that on you when you are singing. You have a kind of, you close your eyes and you sort of listen into yourself. And you can, uh, the one who sees it can well understand that you are listening to what you are going to sing. Now, it must be rather difficult though, to, uh, make music, and also to arrange music, as I see you do, when you don't, can't write. How can you go about it?

Well, you can hear it. You can hear it and you, uh, like my piano player. Now, uh, she can read music. She can sight read and all that, but she, she doesn't have the, uh, she can't, she can't hear what I hear. I can, uh, I can, uh, I hear this music and I go to her and I say, I go to her and, and, and, then she said, well, she said, do that again, do it again, and do it again. And then she, finally she pick it out on the piano. That's how it's done. Yeah, that's what we do it. And then I get another kind of a, like somebody write a song, and the songs sound empty, no feeling. And you know, some people write music, uh, is so dead, that you're, you wouldn't want to hear unless you was in the cemetery, you know. And, uh, I said, oh, a lot could be done with that song. So, uh, uh. You go ahead and do it. Yeah. I go on and and hear something while maybe she's sitting up there playing the notes, playing the piano, just playing. She said, oh, isn't this beautiful? I said, yes, but it's empty. See? Now, just like a, a fella brought a song to me the other day, and he tried to make a song, a prayer, and he tried to make it, uh, semi-classic. So I said, well, he had a little bit of a beat in it, then he had a little sacred, but it wasn't sacred enough for it to mean anything. So I just changed the thing and gave it a real bounce. Ba-da-da-dum-dum-dum-bee-ba-ba-see. That's the song. I didn't call the name of the song because it is mine. But that's the tune we used. It gave it a good bounce, you know. Had the bass going, ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-see. And we went on with the song. The song got a, it was moving pretty good. When we got the same, we got the rocking, you know, moving our bodies like that. And that's how
these things are done. Tell me, I've read somewhere that Bessie Smith

has meant something to you. Well, uh, in the South, in New Orleans where I was born, I didn't get a chance to hear, uh, the great singers like Roland Hayes and, and, um, uh, Grace Moore, Lily Pond, and all those great singers until I came to Chicago up north. Well, we, we did have a chance to hear the blues down there because it's the type of thing that you can hear in the South as soon as you get off the train. People in the South have the, uh, radios or the old-time phonograph just as loud and you can hear the blues. You know, the blues were born in the South and they don't mind playing them and they're not ashamed of it. Everybody, that's one thing that people in the South love the blues and they play it. In fact, all of America loves the blues. And of course, we, um, we got a chance to, uh, to hear more of Bessie Smith. And I suppose basically, uh, that's why so many people say that, uh, I sound like Bessie Smith, but, uh, I suppose I do. She, she was a great singer. It's an honor to sound like her. But, uh, I don't think I sound as great as Bessie. But there, since she's dead, they're giving me the credit that, uh, this is the living Bessie Smith.
But you wouldn't say that you have learned, uh, directly from listening to her. No, no, because

time has advanced so fast. I've had, I've lived up north here for more than 25 years. Now I've had a chance to hear the best of singers and, uh, uh, and to listen to them on radio and television and that the great concerts hold here. Well, I, uh, I, uh, I, uh, I have, I have heard some of the finest artists. But I still think Bessie is a, is a great artist. But I have learned a lot from her time.

I have learned a lot from her. Once before, you and I talked a little about rhythm. In your way of singing, rhythm certainly seems to mean a very great deal. Rhythm is really the heart of the music, isn't it? That's right, that's right. Now, do you feel it helps when you have an audience that

respond even physically? Sure. I don't like to sing to these long hair that, that look like they, they, they can't be moved by music. I believe that any living soul should be moved by music in one way or the other. Everybody's not emotional as I am, but, uh, I like to see people that they, they, there was no more, a beautiful smile come on their face when they hear music. You don't mind their clapping their hands? Oh, no! No, no, no. I think they, they should.
You have traveled a great deal, Miami, haven't you? Yes, I've traveled all over.

I've been everywhere in the United States. And of course, I was in Europe, your part of the country, uh, in 52. Yeah? And I was so well received there. I've sold quite a few records. Um, in Denmark and over in Paris and England, the people were very nice. I remember I went to Denmark for one night and I stayed there five nights. And oh my God, in Paris, you know how they are. They just love music. The English people are very sweet too. You had a very great success in England, didn't you? Yes, I did. Uh, but I, I didn't, I didn't think that I had this, I, I think the success were wonderful for my first time there. I had around 5,000 people. But I, I'm so used to having tremendous crowd in America that I, I thought that Albert Hall should have been packed to 10,000. And the producer, uh, of the, uh, rather the sponsor of the program told me that he thought it was fine for first, making my first appearance in England, you know, to get 5,000 people. Of course, Paris at the L'Isle Playa, I think that's the right name, but it was packed out two nights straight. The right name, but it was packed out two nights straight. And they were very wonderful. And then I went all through the different, uh, uh, towns in France.
Well, you spent some time there in France. Oh yeah, I stayed there six weeks.

And in Europe, six weeks. So are you going back there? Well, I am, uh, I'm now doing local television work and I want to, uh, uh, it seems that I'm just on the verge to get this coast to coast television job. And, um, of course, if I get that, I won't go back to Europe. But if I don't get it, I think I'll even go to Europe again, around, uh, October maybe. I hope for Europe's sake that you will. Oh, I love to go over there. The people are so nice. Now, where would you go if you were to go to Europe? Well, I know I'd, I know I'd have to go back to the places that I first went to. Uh, I had to go back to Denmark. Oh my goodness. I had about, uh, oh, I think I had around 8,000 people there. Um, uh, but, um, it was 4,000 at this, I don't forget the name of the place, but that one, one night was 4,000. And then the, the other than that, the, the church sees around 2,000 called the Holy Ghost Baptist Church. And that church was about 2,000 years old. I, I really was amazed to, to be able to sing in, uh, uh, uh, a church where people, 2,000 years ago, uh, came in and worshiped God. Oh, that was so wonderful to me. I could never get that church out of my mind. Because I never. So you must go back there? Oh, it was just to stand there one more time. That's beautiful. Where else would you go? Oh, I would, when I go back to, uh, uh, to Europe, uh, next time, I'm going to make it my business to just stay there maybe about six months. I just want to, I want to see all the historical things over there. That's the old world, you know. And it's so much different than ours. Everything of them means so much. It, it, it, it, every building over there has, is dedicated to something great that somebody before you have done to make this a great world. You know, it has, it has taught our new world over here, the, the, the, the, the beautiful way of, uh, of, uh, life. And every time you look at one of those buildings, it, you know, somebody great has been there. And you just, you, you, you look like you, you're back into, to history.
You intend to go down to Italy, for instance? Oh, my God, yes, I must go there. Mm-hmm. And I think you said why don't you go to Palestine? Yeah, I want to go to Jerusalem.

It has always been my desire to be in Jerusalem for, uh, Christmas. You know, my Christmas song, Silent Night, which is a European song, sold so many thousand here in America and in Europe. And, um, it was my best song that I, that I sang, because I was there during the cold weather. I was there during October, November. Uh, I, I always wanted to be there since that beautiful song was written. And I understand it was, the song was written not very far from, uh, Bethlehem. Somebody was telling me the story about this song. I have so much to think about that I can't remember right now. But, um, somebody was saying that that, the, the composer didn't live very far from Bethlehem. And I would love to be in Jerusalem on Christmas Eve night. That I well understand. Now tell me, you mentioned a little
while ago that a number of musicians have, uh, wanted you to sing with their bands. Yeah. Armstrong,

for instance. Oh, L. Hines, Duke Ellington, Lionel Hamilton, all of them. You don't want to? No. No. You feel that it wouldn't be right? I do. I really do. Because, um, I feel like this, that no matter how wavered a person might be, they feel that there's a supreme being that is their superior. And they want to always be able to resort to that something as something to lift them up. And it's not this type of work that I do. It is not merely something for entertainment. It is an uplift. It is a reviving for humanity. When man's spirit is low, the, his, his, his divine, uh, savior that he thinks about, he don't want anybody to terminate with that.

Now, I understand so well what you mean. And, uh, I think it's wonderful that you will sing the songs you sing. And, uh, we hope to hear many, many more songs sung by you. We want to hear many more of your beautiful spirituals

songs sung by you. Oh, I love to sing spirituals too. Uh, well, I don't know. I sing the, uh, I sing a lot of the late American, late ballads they got out, like, I Believe and, uh, His Hands. And that's one of my late records on Columbia. I'm now with Columbia records. I was with Apollo for 10 years. Of course, I had a record there that opened the doors for me to the, to, to, to make these big concerts. It was an old time spiritual that I revived with the bounce. Gospel singing just started to having this bounce. And I, uh, was the first one to start this bouncy gospel singing. You know, it was just like a lot of dead music. They used to sing it like everybody was dying or somebody going to a funeral. But, uh, that's when the choir master would sing it. But I always found out that in church service, that the, the convocation or the congregation would always be more jolly and sound better than the choir. That's probably true. Yeah. Yeah. That's because people sing the way it come out of their heart. And the choir always sound dead because the choir director, the person who wrote the music, took all the feeling out of it and made it scientific instead of making it real. And so I, I didn't like the way the choir sang. And so I start to sing it the way I hear the people singing in the congregation in the church around the home. And, of course, leaving the South, coming to Chicago, I started that type of singing. And many people that had left the South, they were living in Chicago. When they heard that type of singing, it was the type that they liked. And that's how I got popular and spread it all over.
Which were your first songs? The ones that really made you famous?

The ones that I came up from New Orleans with. We started to sing an old song about Daniel saw the stone. Now you might hear a choir singing, and they'll sing it so it's with a lot of opera tones to it, you know. But I didn't. I'd sing it, just went on. Oh, Daniel saw the stone that was you'd up to mountain, you'd up to mountain, you'd up to mountain, you'd up to mountain. Daniel saw the stone that was you'd up to mountain, came down to redeem a mighty world. And then it was simple, and the people could catch on. I'd start singing, and everybody in the church. Oh, Daniel saw the stone that was you'd up to mountain, you'd up to mountain. And then the tenor and the sopranos, and all, you know, nobody had, no choir director had to say, now the tenor sang this, the alto sang that, and the bass sang this. They're always bass together without any training, and they come out of their heart. It must be wonderful to sing with that spontaneity. Yeah, I don't like to be, you know, so, so, form. I like to relax myself. And right now, if we start to sing it right now, I bet you the people would come up. And you wouldn't have to tell them what voice to sing it, because their voice would automatically blend in.

Now I'll tell you one thing. The first time I came in to see you, and we started talking, I felt sort of like a dead fish together with you. It was full of life and vitality. But you know, something happened to me while we were talking. Something, this seems to be contagious, you see, this kind of life.
Yeah, people want to be alive. That's right. See that?
I felt much better when I left you. Oh, isn't that wonderful?
I almost get lost in the street among my home.
Well, I think we've got a lot now, don't we?

Well, I'll say this. This new world we are living in is tired of putting on a farm. People wants to live. People wants to enjoy life. And they don't want to go to church and set up and not be a part of the service. I think a whole church should sing, not just the choir. Let everybody sing their song. No care whether it sounds good or bad, that's their song. And they'll feel good trying to sing their song.
I think that's a wonderful idea that we could all be part of.

Do it yourself. Get out and sing yourself. Clap your hands yourself. Dance yourself. And you'll feel better. Don't you? You're right. Sure, I think so. All this informal stuff of you going to church, sitting there, just listening. Be a part of that thing and you can know how glorious it is what you're receiving. That's what I think.

I can remember

quite well quite well. This particular day, a very beautiful day, and the sun was shining, and the people stood all out in the streets, and their faces was very sad. you could hear the church bell ring, and you could hear the screams and the groans of others, especially the family. and I, as a little girl, sensed and felt a sort of sad emotion. I couldn't feel it as deep as the others because I was too small, just about four years old. But I sensed that I had lost someone dear.
